newsitem.title: JORDAN: U.S. envoy says Iraq cutting spending on food.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy says Iraq cutting spending on food.

text.p: The United States deputy representative to the United Nations said on Wednesday Iraq had started to divert money it had previously spent on food rations to other uses since the start of a U.N. oil-for-food deal.
Ambassador Edward Gnehm also dismissed as "propaganda" Iraqi accusations that Washington was holding up food and medicine from reaching Baghdad under the accord.

"We have some evidence that the Iraqi government is not now using its own funds to purchase food but to purchase other things," Gnehm told a satellite news conference beamed to London, Paris, Riyadh, Cairo and Amman.

Gnehm did not elaborate, but he stressed the oil-for-food accord, which allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over a six-month period to pay for food and medicine, was not meant to let Baghdad cut its own contributions to feeding its people.
"We were not trying to substitute for the Iraqi government money that they were already spending on food," he said. "This was to be an additive, not a substitute."
Iraq has suffered crippling trade sanctions since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

The World Health Organisation said last week the country's health system was close to collapse and medicines and other life-saving supplies due to be imported under the oil-for-food deal had failed to arrive.
Iraq says it has submitted 222 contracts for buying food and medicine under the deal, which took effect in early December, but only nine had been approved.
Trade Minister Mohamed Mehdi Saleh accused the United States of practicing genocide against the Iraqi people by delaying the deliveries.

"The remarks that were made by Iraqi officials in the last few weeks I'm afraid I'd put them in the context of propaganda," Gnehm said. "You have to recognise that the government of Iraq on the scene has probably more impact on food and medicine distribution than anyone else."

"The Iraqi government signed a memorandum of understanding with the U.N. to give them free access, free movement, the right to communication...and subsequent to signing the memorandum they backtracked on every one of those," Gnehm said.

But Gnehm said the United Nations was also working to speed up the cumbersome bureaucracy which has slowed food purchases. The purchases have to be approved by a series of committees and can only go ahead when money has been allocated from an escrow account funded by the closely monitored oil sales.

"There are a number of reasons why contracts at the beginning were slow to move. We are trying to break those bureaucratic logjams," Gnehm said. "What we can't do is we can't convince Iraq to stop its own obstruction in the field."
